In the Two Knights Defense ({v1}), the black knight stands on f6 and blocks the queen's diagonal from d8 to g5. Here the diagonal is open, and the knight on g5 is undefended, since the bishop on c1 is still behind the pawn on d2. If White attacks the queen and the bishop on c5 at the same time with {z3}, the queen keeps capturing with {z4} and threatens the rook on h1, which White must rescue with {z5}. Development: White has three minor pieces developed and one traded; Black is still missing the bishop on c8. King safety: neither side has castled yet, but both can do so at once. So Black does worst on the center check, which Black fixes with {z1}: the pawn attacks the pawn on e4 and the bishop on c4 at the same time. After {z2}, White's pawn pair is broken up, and the bishop on c8 has a clear path. On {z3}, Black captures the bishop with {z4} and, after {z5}, stands better, since the isolated pawn on d4 is weak. Almost as good as {z6} is {z7}, which wins the piece back at once. If, on the other hand, Black castles first, White advances with {z8}, and after {z9} White keeps the center and develops in peace. texte.8183792a1db8: In the Queen's Gambit Accepted, Black pays for the pawn's excursion to c4 with time: Black is behind in development and therefore has to play accurately ({z1}, {z2}, {z3}, {z4}). In the Queen's Gambit Declined with the Orthodox Defense, it is the other way round: Black stands firm and is quicker with the king, but has the permanent problem of the bishop on c8. In the Slav Defense ({v1}) this problem does not exist, since the bishop on c8 stays free. There Black reaches all three goals without ever having to shut in a piece ({v2}).
texte.45626ab1eed2: The pawn on d5, plus pressure from c5 and the knight on c6.
texte.c0061819f481: Knights on f3 and d2, bishop on d3; the bishop from c1 was traded.
texte.3c3b388846e5: Knights on c6 and f6, bishop on d7; the bishop from f8 was traded. The rooks are connected.
texte.70f0145f780d: Conclusion: The London System meets the three goals reliably and without risk, which is why it is so popular with beginners. The downside shows as well: White hardly exerts any pressure, and Black has also reached the goals without effort. If you want to win with the London System, you have to do it in the middlegame. The typical plan is the central advance {z1}, which Chapter 5 (Section 5.6) shows in this position.
texte.dbd748416cda: The pawn on d4, supported by e3.
texte.b8866c049f9e: The pawn on d5, defended by the bishop on e6; no pawn can support it any more.
texte.975677a9a6a2: Knights on c3 and e2, bishop on d3; the bishop from c1 was traded.
texte.157159ccd2f2: Knight on c6, bishops on d6 and e6; the knight from f6 was traded.
texte.006151783f09: Conclusion: After ten moves, both sides have reached all three goals ({v1}). The trade on move three shapes the whole position: White plays against the doubled pawns and the pawn on d5, Black wants to open the position for the bishop pair.
texte.a25fd7cc8a66: The chain d4–e5 stands and gains space.
texte.490aab9c260c: The pawn on d5, supported by e6; both knights attack d4.
texte.d5a9cf9fd9b4: Knights on c3 and f3, bishop on e2; the bishop from c1 was traded.
texte.e1fa20ea3ed8: Knights on c6 and f5, bishop on d7; the bishop from f8 was traded. The rooks are connected.
texte.a80f31f06a70: Conclusion: After 13 moves, both sides have reached all three goals ({v1}). The interim position after move eight ({v2}) shows why it took so long: in the closed center there is no threat of a quick attack, and Black needs several moves until the problem child on c8 has also found a square. The bishop on d7, however, remains the most passive piece on the board. Bringing it into play sensibly is the task for the middlegame.
texte.2f997aa1ffc4: The pawn on d5, supported by e6; the knight on c6 attacks d4.
texte.fcc2c7e9b32c: Knights on b3 and f3, bishops on e2 and e3 are developed.
texte.2aaaf97959e9: Knights on c6 and d7, bishops on e7 and f5 are developed; the bishop on f5 stands outside the chain.
texte.b04c0c4db383: Conclusion: After eleven moves, both sides have reached all three goals ({v1}), two moves earlier than in the French Defense. The reason is the early bishop move to f5: Black no longer has a problem child to look after.

texte.0740d35126ed: Conclusion: After 15 moves, both sides have reached all three goals ({v1}). As in the Ruy Lopez, it took longer than ten moves because the center was closed. The fight is now in full swing: White presses with the pawn on e6 and on the queenside, Black seeks play on the kingside.
texte.1c5d1a828c4e: Two Knights Defense: main line after {z1}
texte.e441d70d300c: No center pawn, but the knight on d3 and the bishop on b2 dominate e5 and d4.

texte.b2bd87c755b7: Castled, the pawn shield is intact (h3 has advanced only one square).
texte.5913770b3e66: Conclusion: After 17 moves, both sides have reached all three goals ({v1}), much later than in the quiet openings. The interim position after ten moves ({v2}) shows why: in the Two Knights Defense the fight is first about material and tempo, and only afterwards about development. White keeps the extra pawn, while Black has the more active pieces in return.

texte.876d0b184bbf: Knights on f6 and d7, bishops on d6 and e6 are developed.
texte.d8275387a539: Conclusion: The Bishop's Opening leads to quiet positions in which both sides reach their goals without effort. Black even has a bit more of the center. This fits the description “flexible and solid”: White risks little, but also exerts little pressure.
texte.653c29478b6e: The pawn on d4, isolated, but defended by the knight on f3 and the rook on d1.
texte.625e2ae8b677: No center pawn, but the bishop on b7 and the knights dominate d5, e4 and e5.

texte.8f1d1b76798e: Knights on d7 and f6, bishops on b4 and b7 are developed.
texte.ab6455b7d84a: Conclusion: After twelve moves, both sides have reached all three goals ({v1}). The fight for the center has turned into a fight over the isolated pawn on d4: White has active pieces and open lines in return, Black blockades the square d5 and waits for the endgame, in which the pawn becomes weak.
